title: Ground- and excited-state energies extraction via Trotterization on IBM quantum computers
authors: Fernando Espinoza-Ortiz, Chungwei Lin, Chih-Chun Chien
abstract: We implement the Hadamard test with Trotterized time-evolution operators on IBM quantum computers to simultaneously extract ground- and excited-state energies of the transverse field Ising model (TFIM) and transverse longitudinal field Ising model (TLFIM). The Trotterization circuits for the TFIM admit constant-depth circuits (CDCs) for arbitrary time, allowing us to locate a large number of eigen-energies above the background noise for up to six spins. Via circuit synthesis we show that the three-spin TLFIM has constant-depth structure although it does not meet the known CDC criteria. The CDCs enable the extraction of the ground and first-excited state energies of the three-site TLFIM via its dynamics. We also address complications from the noisy background and discrete Fourier transform to enhance the reliability of the extraction process and compare the results from different generations of IBM hardware to highlight the improvement.
summary: The paper presents a robust method to extract multiple eigenenergies of Ising-type models using noisy IBM quantum computers. It combines Trotterization with the Hadamard test and DFT analysis, achieving significant results by optimizing circuits toward constant depth. This advances the field's capability beyond simple ground-state finding towards full spectral characterization on NISQ devices.
main_problem: The core problem is extracting multiple ground- and excited-state energies of quantum many-body systems using noisy, near-term quantum hardware.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated the reliable extraction of several low-lying eigenenergies for both TFIM and TLFIM on IBM quantum computers, comparing results across different hardware generations.
method: They employ the Hadamard test combined with Trotterized time-evolution operators, followed by a Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) to map the time dynamics back to spectral energies.
model_or_system: The study focuses on simulating the Transverse Field Ising Model (TFIM) and its variant, the Transverse Longitudinal Field Ising Model (TLFIM). These models are implemented on IBM quantum processors using Trotterization circuits optimized for constant depth where possible.
key_observables: Eigenenergies ($E_k$), spectral weights ($|c_k|^2$), and the time-dependent signal $g(t) = \langle\psi|e^{-i \hat{H}t}|\psiangle$.
important_parameters: The analysis involves balancing Trotter error ($\Delta t$) against circuit depth, with specific parameters like $\Delta t/t_0 = 0.1$ (TFIM) and $\Delta t/t_0 = 0.241$ (TLFIM) being crucial.
main_assumptions: The method assumes that the signal can be accurately reconstructed via DFT despite noise, and it relies on optimizing circuits to achieve constant depth where possible.
figures_summary: Figures show Fourier spectra confirming resolved eigenenergies above a calculated noise threshold ($\eta_i$), and comparisons of measured population dynamics $|\langle 0^{\otimes N}|\psi(t)angle|^2$ against high-accuracy classical Runge-Kutta simulations for both TFIM and TLFIM.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the H-test/Trotterization framework, details optimizations like Constant-Depth Circuits (CDCs) for specific Hamiltonians (TFIM), applies this to both TFIM and TLFIM, and concludes by comparing results across different IBM hardware generations against classical benchmarks.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it pushes the boundary of quantum simulation techniques toward extracting detailed spectral information (multiple eigenvalues) rather than just the ground state, which is a major goal for simulating complex Hamiltonians in condensed matter physics.

Figure 3. First and second order Trotterization circuits for a 6-spin TFIM with open boundary condition. Note that the rotation angle for the Rx gates are not the same between circuits. The Rx gates in the second-order Trotterization are θ = −∆t due to the symmetrization in Eq. (6), and the angle in the first-order Trotterization is θ = −2∆t. Meanwhile, the Rzz gates share the same angle θ = −2∆t following equations Eq. (5) and Eq (6).

Figure 4. First and second-order Trotterization circuits for 4-spin TLFIM with open boundary condition. The Rx gates in the second-order Trotterization have angles θ = −∆t due to the symmetrization in Eq. (9), and the angle in the first-order Trotterization is θ = −2∆t. Akin to the TFIM, the Rzz and Rz gates share the same angle θ = −2∆t following Eq. (9).

Figure 5. Fourier spectra of the TFIM with hx/Jz = 1, ∆t/t0 = 0.1, and τ/t0 = 50 for (a) N = 5 and (b) N = 6 spins from IBM Fez and Boston QPUs. The circuits were ran with 6500 shots per circuit to ensure signal resolutions. Each spin simulation consisted of 1002 total circuits; split evenly for extracting the real and imaginary components of the signal. With the guiding state |0⟩⊗N, for N = 5 (N = 6) we can resolve 9 (6) eigenenergies, indicated by the vertial dashed lines. The horizontal dashed lines indicate the background noise threshold according to Eq. (11).

Figure 6. Gate counts versus Trotter steps M for the optimized circuits of the N = 3 TLFIM with second-order Trotterization and ∆t/t0 = 0.241, hx/Jz = 1, and hz/Jz = 0.1. The dashed lines are the gate counts only for the Trotterization of the time-evolution operator after transpilation on IBM Boston, and the solid lines are the gate counts for the controlled unitary for the H-test after transpilation on IBM Boston. For the N = 3 TLFIM, the circuit becomes of constant depth after BQSkit optimization.
